scope: Ten directly inspected source-page commentaries; distinct claims mapped to existing owners. These are targeted topical readings, not exhaustive all-author work collation.
ownerEvidenceScope: Exact source-code lexical references and canonical owner types checked; absence of a title token is not proof a record is missing.
handoffRules: Existing Calendar, Saints, Customs, Sacred Places and Scripture Correspondences owners retain canonical IDs.
Do not treat older processions or lections as binding 1962 rubrics.
Do not create a second saint database or another Atlas.
Website Présentation blocks are editorially anonymous unless separately sourced.
St George and St Christopher legendary cycles stay explicitly identified as legends.

claims.claim: St Blaise's throat-blessing grew from medieval devotion and the tradition of a child rescued from choking on a fishbone; the source distinguishes legendary hagiography from historical cult.
claims.existing: Traditional-year Calendar code explicitly mentions Blaise and throat blessings.
claims.hold: Blessing ritual form/wording requires actual Roman Ritual/approved local practice; do not copy an unverified prayer.

claims.claim: The forty-day Presentation feast is associated with Jerusalem and later Roman adoption; procession/candle customs developed across historical liturgical strata.
claims.existing: Traditional-year Calendar already has Candlemas and procession references.
claims.hold: Site's chronological assertions must be independently verified; older processional forms are not 1962 prescriptions.
claims.sourceTitle: Purification de la T. Sainte Vierge (Présentation du Seigneur)

claims.claim: Rome historically celebrated two stations at the basilicas of Saint Peter at the Vatican and Saint Paul Outside the Walls, with the second station subsequently transferred to 30 June.
claims.existing: Calendar owns fixed 29 June feast and sacred-places registry owns physical place IDs.
claims.hold: Distinct from modern 1962 Mass rubrics; no new duplicate basilica locations.

claims.claim: The liturgical symbolism of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist near the northern summer solstice and Christmas near the winter solstice illustrates John's words 'He must increase, but I must decrease' (John 3:30).
claims.existing: Scripture Correspondences PR #1553 owns typological cross-references and Calendar owns existing John feast.
claims.hold: Symbolic literary interpretation not a physical/astronomical dating assertion about the historical births.

claims.claim: St George's ancient martyr cult and veneration in Rome are historically separable from the later dragon combat imagery.
claims.existing: Living Saints and sacred-art catalogues have separate canonical source owners.
claims.hold: Avoid presenting dragon story as a historically attested event; source site historical dates need critical proof.

claims.claim: The early cult of St Christopher must be distinguished from the western legend of the Christ-bearing giant and east/west legendary embellishments.
claims.existing: Saints profile work includes biography/art differentiation; exact canonical Saint ID not established in this batch.
claims.hold: Legends are symbolism, not documented childhood/birth/death testimony; no invented dates.

claims.claim: St Bonaventure's feast history is presented with canonization in 1482, Doctor of the Church recognition in 1588 and historic feast developments.
claims.existing: Living sanctoral registry controls saint identity and liturgical classification.
claims.hold: Validate canonical saint ID, date and historic feast rank independently before adding to biography.
claims.sourceTitle: St Bonaventure, évêque, confesseur et docteur

claims.claim: Rogation Days are linked to St Mamert at Vienne, penitential processions and supplications for the fruits of the earth; Parsch names Monday station Santa Maria Maggiore.
claims.existing: Calendar customs read model and traditional-year Calendar already reference Rogations and processions.
claims.hold: Distinguish Roman stational history, local processional practice and authorized 1962 rubrics.

claims.claim: Tuesday Rogations station is associated with Saint John Lateran in the historical commentary; Parsch suggests a devotional three-day ordering of intentions.
claims.existing: Rogations custom owner exists; exact Roman location must reuse shared Places ID.
claims.hold: Parsch's devotional suggestion is not a binding liturgical rubric.

claims.claim: Wednesday Rogations station is associated with Saint Peter's Basilica; the commentary situates the Minor Litanies in relation to the Greater Litanies of 25 April.
claims.existing: Rogations custom owner exists; date/context should be distinct from actual procession confirmation.
claims.hold: Historic station assignments may not constitute a 1962 present-day procession schedule.
